abstract_note: Abstract The Mawrth Vallis region is a plateau situated on the highland side of Mars’ hemispheric dichotomy boundary. It has a >200-m-thick phyllosilicate-bearing stratigraphic succession that indicates extensive aqueous alteration between 4.1 Ga and 3.7 Ga, during the Noachian Period. In addition, thousands of kilometre-scale isolated mounds in the lowlands north and west of Mawrth Vallis have been identified. Here we use geomorphological and spectroscopic analyses to show that the mounds are erosional remnants that formed through retreat of the highland plateau in the Noachian. Consequently, the escarpment that marks the surface expression of the dichotomy must have receded south-southeast by hundreds of kilometres in this area. Lateral and stratigraphic geochemical variation in the mounds show that widespread, multiphase aqueous alteration occurred in situ across this region in surface and subsurface environments. The mound succession is underlain by a pyroxene-rich unit that represents unaltered material below the regional phyllosilicate-bearing sequence and is unconformably overlain by a thin capping unit that marks the end of large-scale regional aqueous activity. Thus, the mounds contain a stratigraphic record of the onset, evolution and cessation of Noachian aqueous conditions in this region, detailing the environment and climate of Mars at its most habitable.
research_content: This paper investigates the geomorphology, stratigraphy, and aqueous alteration history of isolated mounds and the highland plateau near Mawrth Vallis on Noachian Mars. The authors used high-resolution remote sensing data, including topographic transects and spectral analyses from CRISM, to demonstrate that the mounds are erosional remnants of a formerly contiguous phyllosilicate-bearing highland plateau that retreated hundreds of kilometers south-southeast. They identified stratigraphic units within the mounds recording a transition from unaltered pyroxene-rich basement to Fe/Mg-smectite-bearing altered strata and a thin capping unit marking the cessation of aqueous alteration. The study reveals multiphase aqueous alteration in surface and subsurface environments and documents large-scale dichotomy boundary retreat and landscape evolution during the Noachian.

query_centered_content: This study provides significant new insights relevant to the question of whether an ancient ocean existed in the Chryse Planitia region of Mars. Through detailed geomorphological, stratigraphic, and spectroscopic analyses of thousands of isolated mounds in the lowlands north and west of Mawrth Vallis—part of the circum-Chryse region—the authors demonstrate that these mounds are erosional remnants of a formerly extensive highland plateau that retreated south-southeast by hundreds of kilometers during the Noachian period. The mounds and the plateau share morphostratigraphic and mineralogical characteristics, including thick (>200 m) phyllosilicate-bearing strata indicative of widespread, multiphase aqueous alteration between ~4.1 and 3.7 Ga. The alteration record includes subsurface reducing environments producing Mg-rich smectites (e.g., saponite) and later surface or near-surface oxidizing conditions forming Fe-rich smectites (e.g., nontronite). The stratigraphy is capped by a thin, non-hydrated unit marking cessation of large-scale aqueous activity. Importantly, the mounds mostly lie topographically below the proposed Noachian 'Arabia' shoreline and above the younger 'Deuteronilus' shoreline, consistent with their formation and erosion occurring during a period compatible with a Noachian ocean undergoing forced regression. The widespread aqueous alteration and the large stratigraphic thickness of altered material across the highland–lowland boundary suggest a coupled hydrological system potentially involving a large standing body of water, such as a northern ocean. However, the authors caution that the escarpment marking the dichotomy boundary has retreated substantially, implying that previously proposed shorelines following this escarpment may not represent original ocean margins. While the data support the plausibility of an ancient ocean facilitating extensive water–rock interactions in Chryse Planitia, the study does not provide direct geomorphic or sedimentological evidence of oceanic shorelines or marine sediments. Alternative alteration processes such as pedogenesis or hydrothermal activity cannot fully explain the observed stratigraphy and mineralogy but may have contributed locally. Thus, this work advances the research status by linking mound formation, aqueous alteration, and dichotomy retreat in a manner consistent with, but not conclusively proving, the existence of a Noachian ocean in Chryse Planitia. The authors highlight the need for future landed missions to these mounds to further constrain the paleoenvironmental conditions and test the ocean hypothesis.
